newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP launches stinging attack on new EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: EP launches stinging attack on new EU treaty.

text.p: The European Parliament launched a blistering attack on Wednesday on a draft of a new European Union treaty due to be signed in Amsterdam next week, saying it failed to go far enough on key issues.

The new treaty falls far short of wide-reaching reforms EU leaders had pledged last year to prepare the 15-member bloc for an ambitious eastwards expansion early next century, the Strasbourg-based assembly said in a highly critical resolution.
The draft, prepared by the Dutch EU presidency, also failed to give the EU enough powers to take joint action on issues close to its citizens' heart, such as jobs, social concerns and foreign policy.
The revised EU treaty expected to be agreed at the June 16-17 summit in Amsterdam looks certain to include for the first time a special chapter on employment, but this did not impress the parliament.
Pauline Green, leader of parliament's largest political party, the Socialists, said it "isn't good enough and it's just pious rhetoric."

Parliament also criticised the draft treaty for failing to make the EU's institutions sufficiently more efficient or democratic, or better able to cope with up to 10 new members from eastern and central Europe.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo staunchly defended the draft, saying a deal in Amsterdam would go much further than anyone believed possible just 18 months ago.
But he conceded that it "won't achieve as much as we'd hoped."

He cautioned that there were limits to what Brussels could do to reduce EU unemployment of 10.9 percent. "It would be very wrong to think that it's the fault of the European Union that there's so much unemployment in Europe," he told parliament.
But "appalling employment figures" had helped EU governments come around to the idea of giving the bloc an employment policy.
Insistence by the new Socialist-led government in France on boosting the role of jobs in plans for economic and monetary union (EMU), were finding echoes in other EU capitals, he added.

While the Dutch EU presidency was pushing for a final deal in Amsterdam, the summit could still be considered a success if EU leaders agreed to the general principles of a new treaty, van Mierlo said.
"The entire package...doesn't need to be identified in Amsterdam," he said.
